stem: An electron moves in a circular orbit of radius 5.0 × 10^-11 m with a speed of 3.0 × 10^6 m/s. Take e = 1.6 × 10^-19 C. The magnetic moment due to this orbital motion is:
explanation: One revolution takes T = 2πr/v, so the equivalent current is I = e/T = ev/(2πr). The magnetic moment is m = I × πr² = evr/2 = (1.6 × 10^-19)(3.0 × 10^6)(5.0 × 10^-11)/2 = 1.2 × 10^-23 A m². Leaving out the factor 1/2 gives 2.4 × 10^-23 A m², which is the value of evr, and 4.8 × 10^-23 doubles it.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 4 Moving Charges and Magnetism: current loop as a magnetic dipole, magnetic moment of a revolving electron

subject: physics
unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
stem: Two long straight parallel wires are 0.40 m apart and carry steady currents of 3 A and 5 A in opposite directions. On the straight line through both wires, the net magnetic field is zero at a distance from the 3 A wire of:
explanation: For opposite currents the two fields add between the wires, so a null point can only lie outside them, beyond the weaker (3 A) wire. With x measured from the 3 A wire, μ0(3)/(2πx) = μ0(5)/(2π(x + 0.40)), so 3(x + 0.40) = 5x and x = 0.60 m. The value 0.15 m is the null point for currents in the same direction, and 1.0 m is the distance of the correct point from the 5 A wire.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 4 Moving Charges and Magnetism: magnetic field of a long straight current-carrying wire and superposition

subject: physics
stem:
Consider the following statements about electromagnetic induction.
(A) The emf induced in a closed loop depends on the resistance of the loop.
(B) An emf can be induced in a coil placed in a steady magnetic field by changing the area of the coil.
(C) One henry is equal to one weber per ampere.
(D) A metal rod at rest in a steady magnetic field has a motional emf between its ends.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
explanation: Induced emf depends on the rate of change of flux, and the resistance of the loop only decides the current, so statement (A) fails. Changing the area changes the flux and induces an emf, and since L = flux/current, 1 H = 1 Wb/A. A rod at rest has v = 0, so its motional emf Blv is zero even in a steady field.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 6 Electromagnetic Induction: Faraday law, motional emf and the unit of inductance

subject: physics
stem: A coil of 100 turns and resistance 20 Ω is linked with a flux that falls from 4.0 × 10^-3 Wb to 1.0 × 10^-3 Wb through each turn in 0.50 s. The total charge that flows through the coil is:
explanation: The charge is q = NΔΦ/R = 100 × (4.0 − 1.0) × 10^-3 / 20 = 1.5 × 10^-2 C, independent of the time taken. Check: emf = 0.30/0.50 = 0.60 V, current = 0.60/20 = 0.030 A, charge = 0.030 × 0.50 = 1.5 × 10^-2 C. The value 3.0 × 10^-2 is the current in amperes, not the charge.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 6 Electromagnetic Induction: induced emf, current and the charge that flows through a coil

subject: physics
stem: The energy stored in the magnetic field of a coil carrying a current of 2 A is 8 J. The self-inductance of the coil is:
explanation: The energy stored in an inductor is U = (1/2) L I². Therefore L = 2U/I² = 2 × 8/2² = 4 H. Check: (1/2) × 4 × 2² = 8 J. Writing U = L I² forgets the factor 1/2 and would give 2 H, while 2U/I gives 8 H because the current is not squared.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 6 Electromagnetic Induction: energy stored in an inductor, U = (1/2) L I²

subject: physics
stem: A square coil of side 10 cm and 100 turns is placed with its plane making an angle of 30° with a uniform magnetic field of 0.20 T. The field is reduced uniformly to zero in 0.010 s. The magnitude of the induced emf is:
explanation: The field makes 30° with the plane, so it makes 60° with the normal and the flux per turn is BA cos 60° = 0.20 × 0.010 × 0.5 = 1.0 × 10^-3 Wb. Then ε = NΔΦ/Δt = 100 × 1.0 × 10^-3 / 0.010 = 10 V. Using cos 30° treats the given angle as the one with the normal and gives 10√3 V, while taking the field as perpendicular gives 20 V.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 6 Electromagnetic Induction: magnetic flux through a tilted coil and Faraday law

subject: physics
stem: A lamp rated 100 W at 100 V is to be operated from a 125 V AC supply, with a pure inductor connected in series so that the lamp works at its rated power. The inductive reactance of the inductor must be:
explanation: The lamp resistance is R = V²/P = 100²/100 = 100 Ω and its rated current is 100/100 = 1 A. The circuit must have Z = 125/1 = 125 Ω, so X_L = √(Z² − R²) = √(125² − 100²) = 75 Ω. Subtracting the resistances gives 25 Ω, but resistance and reactance combine at right angles, and adding the squares instead of subtracting them gives 160 Ω.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 7 Alternating Current: resistance and reactance in series, impedance Z = √(R² + X²)

subject: physics
stem: A series LCR circuit is connected to a 100 V (rms) AC source. The resistance is 30 Ω, the inductive reactance is 80 Ω and the capacitive reactance is 40 Ω. The rms voltage across the inductor is:
explanation: The impedance is Z = √(R² + (XL − XC)²) = √(30² + 40²) = 50 Ω, so I = 100/50 = 2 A and VL = I × XL = 2 × 80 = 160 V. This is larger than the supply because VL and VC are in antiphase: the phasor sum is √(60² + (160 − 80)²) = 100 V. Taking 100 V assumes no part can exceed the source, which holds only for in-phase voltages.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 7 Alternating Current: series LCR circuit, phasors, impedance and component voltages

subject: physics
stem: The emf of an AC generator varies as e = e0 sin ωt and the frequency is 50 Hz. Starting from e = 0, the time taken for the emf to first reach half of its peak value e0 is:
explanation: When e = e0/2, sin ωt = 1/2, so ωt = π/6. With ω = 2π × 50 = 100π rad/s, t = (π/6)/(100π) = 1/600 s. A time of 1/300 s corresponds to ωt = π/3 (the sine of 60°), 1/200 s is the quarter period needed to reach the peak, and 1/100 s is the half period.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 7 Alternating Current: AC generator, instantaneous emf e = e0 sin ωt

stem:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I: (A) Radio waves (B) Infrared waves (C) X-rays (D) Gamma rays
List-II: (I) High-energy electrons striking a metal target (II) Transitions of excited atomic nuclei (III) Rapid acceleration and deceleration of electrons in an aerial (IV) Vibrations of atoms and molecules in hot bodies
Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
explanation: Radio waves come from rapid acceleration and deceleration of electrons in an aerial, infrared from vibrating atoms and molecules in hot bodies, X-rays from high-energy electrons striking a metal target, and gamma rays from excited nuclei. A common slip is to swap X-rays and gamma rays, which differ in origin: electron collisions with matter against nuclear transitions.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 8 Electromagnetic Waves: sources of the electromagnetic spectrum

stem:
Arrange the following electromagnetic radiations in decreasing order of frequency.
(A) Infrared rays
(B) Gamma rays
(C) Microwaves
(D) Ultraviolet rays
Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
explanation: Frequency rises along the spectrum in the order radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays. In decreasing order of frequency the four given radiations are gamma rays, ultraviolet, infrared and microwaves. Reading the spectrum from the low-frequency end gives the exact reverse, the usual slip when the direction asked for is missed.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 8 Electromagnetic Waves: the electromagnetic spectrum in order of frequency

subject: physics
stem: The magnetic field amplitude of a plane electromagnetic wave in vacuum is 2.0 × 10^-7 T. Take c = 3.0 × 10^8 m/s. The amplitude of its electric field is:
explanation: In vacuum the amplitudes of an electromagnetic wave are related by E0/B0 = c, so E0 = cB0 = 3.0 × 10^8 × 2.0 × 10^-7 = 60 V/m. Dividing B0 by c gives 6.7 × 10^-16, which inverts the relation, and multiplying by c twice overshoots to 1.8 × 10^10.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 8 Electromagnetic Waves: characteristics of electromagnetic waves, E0/B0 = c

stem:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I: (A) Silicon doped with arsenic (B) Silicon doped with indium (C) p-n junction under forward bias (D) p-n junction under reverse bias
List-II: (I) Holes are the majority carriers (II) Narrow depletion layer and large current (III) Electrons are the majority carriers (IV) Wide depletion layer and very small current
Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
explanation: Arsenic has five valence electrons and makes silicon n-type, with electrons as the majority carriers; indium has three and makes it p-type, with holes as the majority carriers. Forward bias narrows the depletion layer and gives a large current, whereas reverse bias widens it and gives only a very small current. Swapping the two dopants is the common slip.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 14 Semiconductor Electronics: n-type and p-type doping, p-n junction under forward and reverse bias

subject: physics
stem: In terms of energy bands, a metallic conductor is characterised by:

options.text: a full valence band and an empty conduction band, separated by a gap of more than 3 eV
a full valence band and an empty conduction band, separated by a gap of about 1 eV
a full conduction band and an empty valence band, separated by a small gap
a conduction band that is partly filled or overlaps the valence band

explanation: In a metal the conduction band is partly filled, or overlaps the valence band, so electrons can move under a field without needing extra energy. A full valence band with a gap above 3 eV describes an insulator, and a gap of about 1 eV describes an intrinsic semiconductor such as silicon.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 14 Semiconductor Electronics: energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators

subject: physics
stem: In a doped silicon sample the electron concentration is 4.0 × 10^22 m^-3. The intrinsic carrier concentration of silicon is 2.0 × 10^16 m^-3. The hole concentration in the sample is:
explanation: In a doped semiconductor n_e × n_h = n_i². So n_h = (2.0 × 10^16)² / (4.0 × 10^22) = 4.0 × 10^32 / 4.0 × 10^22 = 1.0 × 10^10 m^-3. Donor doping raises the electrons and suppresses the holes far below n_i, so keeping the value n_i is wrong, as is multiplying n_e by n_i.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 14 Semiconductor Electronics: intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, n_e n_h = n_i²

subject: physics
stem: In an unbiased p-n junction at equilibrium, the net current across the junction is zero because:

options.text: the diffusion current of majority carriers is balanced by the drift current of minority carriers
the depletion layer stops the majority carriers and the minority carriers from crossing the junction
the potential barrier across the junction vanishes once the equilibrium is reached
the p-side and the n-side contain equal numbers of holes and of electrons

explanation: Diffusion of majority carriers across the junction builds the depletion layer and its barrier field, and this field drives minority carriers the other way as the drift current. At equilibrium the two currents are equal and opposite, so the net current is zero. The barrier potential does not vanish, and the layer does not stop all crossing, because carriers move in both directions.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 14 Semiconductor Electronics: p-n junction formation, diffusion and drift currents, depletion layer

subject: physics
stem: A silicon diode, which drops 0.7 V when it conducts, is connected in the forward direction in series with a 1.0 kΩ resistor and a 5.7 V battery. The current in the circuit is:
explanation: A conducting silicon diode drops 0.7 V, so the resistor has 5.7 − 0.7 = 5.0 V across it and I = 5.0/1000 = 5.0 mA. Check: 5.0 mA × 1.0 kΩ + 0.7 V = 5.7 V. Ignoring the diode drop gives 5.7 mA, while subtracting 0.7 twice gives 4.3 mA.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 14 Semiconductor Electronics: p-n junction diode in forward bias, forward voltage drop

subject: physics
stem: A pebble lies at the bottom of a pool of water (refractive index 4/3) that is 2.4 m deep. Seen from directly above, the pebble appears to be raised by:
explanation: For near-normal viewing the apparent depth is real depth/μ = 2.4/(4/3) = 1.8 m, so the pebble appears raised by 2.4 − 1.8 = 0.6 m. The value 1.8 m is the apparent depth itself, not the shift, and 0.8 m comes from wrongly using d(μ − 1) for the shift.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 9 Ray Optics and Optical Instruments: refraction at a plane surface and the apparent depth of an object under water

subject: physics
stem: A point object is placed on the axis in air, 60 cm in front of a convex spherical glass surface (μ = 1.5) of radius of curvature 15 cm. The distance of the image from the surface is:
explanation: For refraction at a single spherical surface, μ2/v − μ1/u = (μ2 − μ1)/R. With u = −60 cm and R = +15 cm, 1.5/v + 1/60 = 0.5/15 = 1/30, so 1.5/v = 1/60 and v = +90 cm, a real image inside the glass. Writing 1/v in place of 1.5/v, as for a lens, gives the tempting 60 cm.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 9 Ray Optics and Optical Instruments: refraction at a spherical surface

subject: physics
stem: A compound microscope has an objective of focal length 1.0 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5.0 cm, and its tube length (distance between the inner focal points) is 20 cm. For the final image at infinity, the magnifying power is (D = 25 cm):
explanation: With the final image at infinity, M = (L/fₒ)(D/fₑ) = (20/1.0)(25/5.0) = 20 × 5 = 100. The factor (1 + D/fₑ) = 6 gives 120, but that belongs to a final image at the near point, and 130 comes from using the 26 cm lens separation as if it were the tube length.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 9 Ray Optics and Optical Instruments: compound microscope, tube length and magnifying power

subject: physics
stem: Two thin prisms are joined with their refracting edges pointing in opposite directions. One has angle 6° and refractive index 1.5; the other has angle 4° and refractive index 1.6. The net deviation of a ray passing through the combination is:
explanation: A thin prism deviates a ray by δ = (μ − 1)A, giving 0.5 × 6° = 3.0° and 0.6 × 4° = 2.4°. The prisms are inverted relative to each other, so the deviations subtract: 3.0° − 2.4° = 0.6°. Adding them gives 5.4°, and using μA instead of (μ − 1)A gives 2.6°.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 9 Ray Optics and Optical Instruments: refraction through a thin prism, deviation δ = (μ − 1)A

subject: physics
stem:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I: (A) Signal transmission through an optical fibre (B) Image formation by a convex lens (C) Image formation by a plane mirror (D) Splitting of white light by a glass prism
List-II: (I) Reflection (II) Total internal reflection (III) Dispersion (IV) Refraction
Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
explanation: An optical fibre guides light by repeated total internal reflection, a convex lens forms its image by refraction at its two surfaces, a plane mirror forms its image by reflection, and a prism spreads white light into colours by dispersion because the refractive index varies with wavelength. Pairing the prism with refraction is tempting since the light bends at its faces, but the colour spread is specifically dispersion.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 9 Ray Optics and Optical Instruments: reflection, refraction, total internal reflection (optical fibres) and dispersion as the principles of optical devices

subject: physics
stem: A point source of light is placed at the principal focus of a thin convex lens. The wavefront of the light emerging from the lens is:
explanation: Rays from a source at the focus leave the lens parallel to the principal axis, and wavefronts are perpendicular to the rays, so the emerging wavefront is plane. A diverging spherical wavefront is what the source itself emits before the lens, while a converging one forms when a parallel beam enters the lens.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 10 Wave Optics: wavefronts and Huygens principle, wavefront shape after a lens

subject: physics
stem: A plane wavefront travelling in air meets the surface of a transparent medium at an angle of incidence of 60°. The speed of light in the medium is c/√3. The angle of refraction is:
explanation: In Huygens’ construction the wavefront turns because its speed changes: sin i / sin r = v1/v2 = c/(c/√3) = √3. So sin r = sin 60°/√3 = (√3/2)/√3 = 1/2 and r = 30°. Dividing the angle itself, 60°/√3 ≈ 35°, treats the angle as proportional to the speed ratio, which Snell’s law does not.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 10 Wave Optics: refraction of a plane wave at a plane surface using Huygens principle

subject: physics
stem: Light of wavelength 400 nm falls on two narrow slits 0.6 mm apart, and the fringes are viewed on a screen 1.5 m away. On one side of the central maximum, the third dark fringe lies at what distance from the centre?
explanation: The fringe width is β = λD/d = (400 × 10⁻⁹ × 1.5)/(0.6 × 10⁻³) = 1.0 mm. Dark fringes lie at (n − ½)β from the centre, so the third (n = 3) is at 2.5β = 2.5 mm. The distance 3.0 mm marks the third bright fringe, which sits beyond the dark fringe.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 10 Wave Optics: Young’s double-slit experiment, positions of dark fringes and fringe width

subject: physics
stem: In a Young’s double-slit experiment the slit separation and the screen distance are kept fixed. Arrange the following monochromatic lights in increasing order of fringe width: (A) Green light (B) Red light (C) Violet light (D) Yellow light
explanation: The fringe width β = λD/d is directly proportional to the wavelength when D and d are fixed. Wavelength increases through violet, green, yellow and red, so the fringe widths follow the same order. Swapping green and yellow reverses their true wavelength order, and the reverse of the correct ordering would give decreasing fringe width.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 10 Wave Optics: fringe width in Young’s experiment, dependence on wavelength and the order of colours in the visible spectrum

subject: physics
unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
stem: A neutron of mass 1.65 × 10^-27 kg moves with a speed of 4.0 × 10^3 m s^-1. Taking h = 6.6 × 10^-34 J s, its de Broglie wavelength is:
explanation: The de Broglie wavelength is λ = h/p = h/(mv). Here p = 1.65 × 10^-27 × 4.0 × 10^3 = 6.6 × 10^-24 kg m s^-1, so λ = 6.6 × 10^-34 / 6.6 × 10^-24 = 1.0 × 10^-10 m. Treating the momentum as mv² instead of mv would give about 2.5 × 10^-14 m.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 11 Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter: matter waves and the de Broglie relation λ = h/mv

subject: physics
unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
stem: A lamp radiates 3.3 W of monochromatic light of wavelength 600 nm. Taking h = 6.6 × 10^-34 J s and c = 3.0 × 10^8 m s^-1, the number of photons emitted per second is about:
explanation: The energy of one photon is E = hc/λ = (6.6 × 10^-34 × 3.0 × 10^8)/(6.0 × 10^-7) = 3.3 × 10^-19 J. The number emitted per second is N = P/E = 3.3/(3.3 × 10^-19) = 1.0 × 10^19. Writing 600 nm as 6 × 10^-6 m instead of 6 × 10^-7 m gives 1.0 × 10^20.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 11 Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter: particle nature of light, photon energy E = hc/λ

subject: physics
unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
stem: For a photosensitive metal, the stopping potential is V0 for light of wavelength λ and 3V0 for light of wavelength λ/2. The threshold wavelength of the metal is:
explanation: Einstein’s equation gives eV0 = hc/λ − φ and 3eV0 = 2hc/λ − φ. Subtracting, hc/λ = 2eV0, so φ = hc/λ − eV0 = eV0 = hc/(2λ), and the threshold wavelength is hc/φ = 2λ. Reading the 3 : 1 ratio of stopping potentials as a ratio of wavelengths gives 3λ, which ignores the work function.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 11 Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter: Einstein’s photoelectric equation, stopping potential, work function and threshold wavelength

subject: physics
stem:
Match List-I (quantity for the nth Bohr orbit of hydrogen) with List-II (dependence on n).
List-I: (A) Radius of the orbit (B) Speed of the electron (C) Magnitude of the total energy (D) Angular momentum of the electron
List-II: (I) Proportional to 1/n² (II) Proportional to n (III) Proportional to 1/n (IV) Proportional to n²
Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
explanation: In the Bohr model the radius varies as n², the speed as 1/n, the total energy as −13.6 eV/n² so its magnitude varies as 1/n², and the angular momentum is nh/2π, proportional to n. A student who pairs the speed with 1/n² has carried the energy dependence across, since speed falls only as 1/n.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 12 Atoms: Bohr model of the hydrogen atom, radius, speed, energy and angular momentum of the nth orbit

subject: physics
stem: An alpha particle of kinetic energy 7.2 MeV approaches a tin nucleus (atomic number 50) head-on. Taking e²/(4πε₀) = 1.44 MeV fm, the distance of closest approach is:
explanation: At the closest approach all the kinetic energy has become electrostatic potential energy: K = (2e)(Ze)/(4πε₀r₀), so r₀ = 2Z × 1.44 MeV fm / K = (2 × 50 × 1.44)/7.2 = 20 fm. Leaving out the charge 2e of the alpha particle gives 10 fm.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 12 Atoms: alpha-particle scattering, Rutherford model and the distance of closest approach

subject: physics
stem: A sample of hydrogen atoms has all its electrons excited to the n = 4 level. The maximum number of different spectral lines that can be emitted as the atoms return to lower levels is:
explanation: Spectral lines arise from transitions between pairs of levels, and four levels give n(n − 1)/2 = 4 × 3/2 = 6 pairs: 4→3, 4→2, 4→1, 3→2, 3→1 and 2→1. Counting only the three drops from n = 4 (n − 1) misses the lines from the intermediate cascades.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 12 Atoms: energy level transitions and hydrogen line spectra

subject: physics
stem: In the hydrogen spectrum, the ratio of the longest wavelength of the Balmer series to the shortest wavelength of the Paschen series is:
explanation: With E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV and wavelength inversely proportional to the photon energy, the longest Balmer wavelength comes from 3 to 2: dE = 13.6(1/4 - 1/9) = 13.6 x 5/36 eV, and the shortest Paschen wavelength from infinity to 3: dE = 13.6/9 eV. The wavelength ratio is (1/9)/(5/36) = 4/5, so 4 : 5. Comparing the two series limits (dE = 13.6/4 against 13.6/9) instead gives 4 : 9.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 12 Atoms: hydrogen line spectra, Balmer and Paschen series and the Rydberg formula

subject: physics
stem: Which one of the following pairs of nuclides consists of isotones?
explanation: Isotones have the same number of neutrons, N = A − Z. C-13 has 13 − 6 = 7 neutrons and N-14 has 14 − 7 = 7. H-3 and He-3 share the mass number (isobars), C-12 and C-14 share the atomic number (isotopes), and N-14 and O-16 have 7 and 8 neutrons respectively.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 13 Nuclei: composition of the nucleus, isotopes, isobars and isotones

subject: physics
stem: A nuclear reactor delivers 3.2 MW of power from the fission of uranium, each fission releasing 200 MeV. Taking 1 MeV = 1.6 × 10^-13 J, the number of fissions per second is:
explanation: The energy per fission is 200 × 1.6 × 10^-13 = 3.2 × 10^-11 J. The fission rate is P/E = 3.2 × 10^6 / 3.2 × 10^-11 = 1.0 × 10^17 per second. Treating the energy as 200 eV instead of 200 MeV (a factor of 10^6) would give 1.0 × 10^23.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 13 Nuclei: nuclear fission and the energy released per fission

subject: physics
stem: The binding energy per nucleon is 1.1 MeV for deuterium (H-2) and 7.1 MeV for helium (He-4). The energy released when two deuterium nuclei fuse to form one helium nucleus is:
explanation: The energy released equals the binding energy of the product minus that of the reactants. He-4 has 4 × 7.1 = 28.4 MeV and the two H-2 nuclei have 2 × (2 × 1.1) = 4.4 MeV, so Q = 28.4 − 4.4 = 24.0 MeV. Subtracting the per-nucleon values (6.0 MeV) ignores the number of nucleons, and quoting 28.4 MeV forgets that the deuterons were already bound.
ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 13 Nuclei: binding energy, nuclear fusion and energy released
